purpose: Follow-up experiments run after the original 01-09 pipeline was complete, in response to a review asking whether validation PR-AUC (0.1959, tuned Random Forest) or calibration (previously undone) could be improved. Recorded here -- including the negative results -- so nobody re-runs the same four experiments in six months expecting a different answer.
protocol: Same discipline as Notebook 06/07: fit on X_train_tree_based / y_train only, select on X_val_tree_based / y_val PR-AUC. Test set was NOT touched for any of this -- it stays a one-time evaluation per split_config.json.

experiments.name: HistGradientBoosting, broader RandomizedSearchCV
experiments.method: 40-iteration random search over max_iter/max_depth/learning_rate/max_leaf_nodes/min_samples_leaf/l2_regularization/class_weight, TimeSeriesSplit(5) scored on PR-AUC, fit on train only.
experiments.verdict: Worse than baseline RF. Confirms Notebook 06/08's finding that boosting methods underperform RF on this feature set, now under a wider search too -- not just under-tuned.

experiments.name: Random Forest, broader RandomizedSearchCV than the original Optuna run
experiments.method: 10-iteration random search (single-core budget) over n_estimators/max_depth/min_samples_leaf/min_samples_split/max_features/class_weight, TimeSeriesSplit(3), fit on train only.
experiments.verdict: Worse than baseline. Notebook 07's Optuna run (TPE sampler, larger trial budget) found a better point than a quick random search reproduces -- evidence the original tuning was a genuine optimum for this search space, not a lucky seed.

experiments.name: Probability-weighted ensemble: tuned RF + tuned Logistic Regression
experiments.method: Weighted average of predict_proba outputs, weights swept 0.3-0.9 on RF; also tried rank-average blending.
experiments.result: PR-AUC strictly increases as RF weight -> 1.0 (best blend at RF=0.9 still only 0.1937); no blend beat pure RF.
experiments.verdict: LR is not diverse/strong enough at this task to add ranking value on top of RF. Do not ensemble these two for production.

experiments.name: Hand-crafted interaction features (macro_stress_index, contacted_x_poutcome_success, campaign_x_previous), same tuned RF hyperparameters
experiments.verdict: Worse than baseline both ways. RF's own feature-subsampling already captures these interactions; adding redundant/noisy engineered columns diluted split quality rather than helping. Not recommended.

experiments.name: Probability calibration: CalibratedClassifierCV (isotonic and sigmoid), 5-fold, tuned RF hyperparameters, fit on train only
experiments.verdict: Real trade-off, not a wash. Calibration cuts Brier score by ~65% (0.335 -> ~0.118) -- probabilities become genuinely more literal -- but costs 42-54% of ranking quality (PR-AUC 0.196 -> 0.09-0.11). Cause: CalibratedClassifierCV's internal 5-fold refit each sees only 80% of an already-small positive class (~1,600 positives train-wide), which measurably hurts ranking even though it fixes probability magnitude.
experiments.recommendation: DO NOT calibrate the production model. The deployment operating point (models/predict.py, model_card.json) is rank/percentile-based (top-K%) specifically because raw probabilities aren't trustworthy across the regime shift documented in split_config.json -- that design decision means ranking quality (PR-AUC) is what matters operationally, not Brier score. Calibration would be the right move only if a future version switches to a fixed-probability decision rule, which is not recommended here for the reason above. This supersedes the model card's previous one-line 'not calibrated' caveat with a tested, quantified reason.

overall_conclusion: Four independent attempts to beat the Notebook 07 tuned Random Forest (broader boosting search, broader RF search, ensembling, feature engineering) all underperformed it on validation PR-AUC, and calibration was tested and explicitly rejected for the ranking use case. This is treated as reasonably strong (not proof-positive) evidence that 0.1959 is close to what this feature set / algorithm family can extract from this data, given the constraints already documented elsewhere (crisis-period train/test regime shift, duration excluded as leakage, ~6-11% base rate). Further gains are more likely to come from new data (richer behavioral/RFM features, a longer or more balanced time window) than from more modeling effort on the current feature set.
